title: Non-standard memory models with indexed retrieval
summary: The standard memory models for neural networks are variants of the Hopfield network, where feature representations are stored as vectors in a matrix. Retrieval happens based on similarity between an input vector and the set of stored vectors in a content-addressable manner such that the network evolves towards the closest stored attractor. In other words, the useful property of addressing items in memory directly by index is lost in Hopfield-style neural network models ("associative memory"). In this extended abstract, we present a new model which is extremely simple, derived from biological observation, yet introduces a significant conceptual advance and technical benefits. The goal is to establish adaptivity based on the neuron-centric hypothesis: Plasticity is organized by the neuron which regulates its own synapses. Accordingly we implemented a localist, neuron-centric one-shot learning method and applied it to a simple pattern classification problem (MNIST). We were looking for the existence of high information neurons, to act as indices into the representations. The idea was that we would be able to restore full patterns by indexed retrieval, instead of associative vector retrieval from attractors.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a neuron-centric, localist one-shot learning model inspired by biological observations, where individual neurons regulate their own synapses to act as indices for memory retrieval. Unlike standard Hopfield-style associative memory networks that retrieve via attractor dynamics, this model enables direct indexed retrieval of stored patterns, applied to MNIST classification.
AI.motivation: Standard neural network memory models based on Hopfield networks use associative memory where retrieval is based on similarity to stored attractors, losing the ability to directly address items by index. The authors seek to restore indexed retrieval based on the neuron-centric hypothesis that plasticity is organized by individual neurons regulating their own synapses.
AI.method: The authors implement a localist, neuron-centric one-shot learning method where individual neurons act as indices into stored representations. The approach seeks high information neurons that can serve as indices, enabling full patterns to be restored via indexed retrieval rather than associative vector retrieval from attractors. The model is tested on MNIST pattern classification.
AI.result: The paper presents a conceptual advance toward indexed retrieval in neural memory models, demonstrating the existence of high information neurons that can act as indices into representations, applied to MNIST classification.
AI.conclusion: The neuron-centric, localist one-shot learning approach represents a significant conceptual shift from Hopfield-style associative memory, potentially enabling efficient indexed retrieval in neural networks while being grounded in biological observation.

title: Multiscale Community-Based Fingerprinting of Signed Functional Networks
summary: Objective: Recent studies demonstrate that functional connectomes contain subject-specific signatures, or \textit{fingerprints}, that can identify individuals across repeated sessions and tasks. Existing methods mostly rely on edge-level features that are sensitive to noise, difficult to interpret, and limited in their ability to generalize across tasks and datasets. Methods: We propose a multiscale community-based functional connectome fingerprinting framework that characterizes each individual by the mesoscale structure of their functional networks. We introduce a signed multilayer community detection framework that incorporates both correlated and anti-correlated brain activity to identify subject-specific community structures across tasks and sessions. Graph-theoretic metrics are then computed from the resulting joint community structures to derive low-dimensional community-level fingerprint representations. Results: The proposed framework is evaluated on 810 healthy control subjects from the Human Connectome Project (HCP). The results show that community-based fingerprints provide a reliable and interpretable substrate for individualized brain characterization across sessions and tasks. Conclusion: Mesoscale community structure provides meaningful and discriminative subject-specific fingerprints. Significance: The proposed framework offers a promising foundation for precision neuroimaging and personalized neuroscience applications.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a multiscale community-based functional connectome fingerprinting framework that uses signed multilayer community detection, incorporating both correlated and anti-correlated brain activity, to derive low-dimensional subject-specific fingerprints from mesoscale network structure. Evaluated on 810 HCP subjects, community-based fingerprints prove reliable and interpretable for identifying individuals across sessions and tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing functional connectome fingerprinting methods rely on edge-level features that are noise-sensitive, difficult to interpret, and generalize poorly across tasks and datasets. A need exists for more robust and interpretable subject-specific brain signatures.
AI.method: A signed multilayer community detection framework is introduced that incorporates both correlated and anti-correlated brain activity. Multiscale community-based fingerprinting characterizes individuals via mesoscale network structure, and graph-theoretic metrics computed from joint community structures yield low-dimensional community-level fingerprint representations.
AI.result: Evaluated on 810 healthy controls from the Human Connectome Project, community-based fingerprints provide reliable and interpretable subject-specific characterization across sessions and tasks.
AI.conclusion: Mesoscale community structure provides meaningful and discriminative subject-specific fingerprints, offering a promising foundation for precision neuroimaging and personalized neuroscience.

authors: Sjors G. J. G. In 't Veld
title: A Correspondence Score for Validating Learned Patient Representations in Clinical Tabular Data
summary: Identifying patients with similar clinical characteristics is important for cohort discovery, clinical decision support, and personalized medicine. However, it is unclear whether learned patient representations preserve the similarities present in the original clinical data. We propose a correspondence score to directly assess how well these relationships are preserved, independently of labeled outcomes. The score combines complementary relationship-preservation metrics, with dataset-specific weights estimated through Bayesian optimization. We evaluated the approach on four complete blood count datasets using representations generated by five tabular foundation models and six classical transformation methods. Correspondence differed substantially across methods and representation dimensionalities. Patient relationships were generally best preserved at intermediate dimensionalities, while stronger reduction or expansion introduced greater deviations from the original data structure. Foundation models preserved correspondence more consistently than classical methods, with improvements ranging from approximately 5% to over 125%. The proposed score provides a way to evaluate representation quality before downstream use and supports informed selection of representation methods and dimensionalities.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a correspondence score to evaluate whether learned patient representations preserve similarity relationships from original clinical data, using Bayesian-optimized weights for complementary metrics. Evaluated on complete blood count datasets across tabular foundation models and classical methods, intermediate dimensionalities and foundation models best preserve patient relationships.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether learned patient representations preserve the similarity relationships present in original clinical data, which is critical for downstream applications like cohort discovery and personalized medicine. There is a need for an outcome-independent method to directly assess relationship preservation.
AI.method: A correspondence score that combines complementary relationship-preservation metrics, with dataset-specific weights estimated via Bayesian optimization. The approach was evaluated on four complete blood count datasets using representations from five tabular foundation models and six classical transformation methods across varying dimensionalities.
AI.result: Correspondence differed substantially across methods and dimensionalities. Intermediate dimensionalities best preserved patient relationships, while extreme reduction/expansion introduced deviations. Foundation models preserved correspondence more consistently than classical methods, with improvements ranging from ~5% to over 125%.
AI.conclusion: The proposed correspondence score enables evaluation of representation quality before downstream use and supports informed selection of representation methods and dimensionalities for patient similarity tasks.

title: CIR-DDG: backbone-agnostic residual correction of antibody-antigen affinity changes with explicit cross-chain geometry
summary: Motivation: Accurate prediction of mutation-induced protein--protein binding free-energy changes is important for antibody affinity maturation, yet scarce labels and complex interface geometry limit generalization. Heterogeneous predictors may process three-dimensional complexes without preserving the cross-chain signals most relevant to a mutation in their final scalar output. Results: We introduce CIR-DDG, a lightweight residual adapter that combines a fixed base prediction with 22 interpretable descriptors of cross-chain distance, contact density and site--partner context. In complex-level five-fold evaluation on SKEMPI 2.0 measurements from 343 complexes, CIR-DDG improved all six tested backbones on antibody--antigen interface mutations: Spearman correlation increased by 0.0346--0.1296, while RMSE decreased by 0.0074--0.0408\kcalmol. Cross-validated probing, equal-capacity controls and feature ablations support the complementarity of explicit geometry. On an independent SARS-CoV-2 RBD--ACE2 deep-mutational-scan benchmark of 3669 substitutions, the fold-specific adapters transferred without any retraining: the absolute interface Spearman correlation increased by 0.026--0.081 for all four evaluable backbones, showing that the learned geometric correction generalizes beyond SKEMPI thermodynamic measurements. Availability and implementation: CIR-DDG is available at https://github.com/ecnuabmlab/CIR-ddG.

AI.tldr: CIR-DDG is a lightweight residual adapter that combines a fixed base prediction with 22 interpretable cross-chain geometric descriptors, improving mutation-induced protein-protein binding free-energy change prediction across six backbones on SKEMPI 2.0 and generalizing to an independent SARS-CoV-2 RBD-ACE2 benchmark.
AI.motivation: Accurate prediction of mutation-induced binding free-energy changes is important for antibody affinity maturation, but scarce labels and complex interface geometry limit generalization. Existing predictors may process 3D complexes without preserving the most relevant cross-chain signals in their final scalar output.
AI.method: CIR-DDG combines a fixed base prediction with 22 interpretable descriptors of cross-chain distance, contact density, and site-partner context via a lightweight residual adapter.
AI.result: On SKEMPI 2.0 (343 complexes, five-fold), CIR-DDG improved all six backbones on antibody-antigen mutations: Spearman rose 0.0346-0.1296 and RMSE dropped 0.0074-0.0408 kcal/mol. On an independent SARS-CoV-2 RBD-ACE2 DMS benchmark (3669 substitutions), fold-specific adapters transferred without retraining, improving absolute interface Spearman by 0.026-0.081 for all four evaluable backbones.
AI.conclusion: Cross-validated probing, equal-capacity controls, and feature ablations support the complementarity of explicit geometry, and the learned geometric correction generalizes beyond SKEMPI thermodynamic measurements.

title: Two blind spots in the demographic inference of human origins from genomic data
summary: Ancient DNA and new inference methods have transformed the study of human origins, but consensus has not followed. Evidence increasingly indicates that hominin populations were pervasively structured and admixed, so complexity rather than simplicity is the appropriate prior. Here I highlight two blind spots that impede resolving that complexity. First, every inference passes through summaries of the data, and those summaries bound what can be recovered. Second, the space of candidate models is vast, yet competing model classes are rarely fit to common data, so a reported best model carries little evidence about untested model classes. This second blind spot reflects practice rather than data. It can be narrowed by testing competing models against withheld summaries and by reporting the models that were tried and rejected rather than only the winner.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that while ancient DNA and new inference methods have revolutionized human origins research, two blind spots impede resolving the complexity of hominin population history: (1) data summaries bound what can be recovered from the data, and (2) the vast model space means reported "best" models carry little evidence about untested model classes. The second blind spot can be narrowed by testing competing models against withheld summaries and reporting models that were tried and rejected.
AI.motivation: To address why consensus has not followed the transformative advances in ancient DNA and inference methods for studying human origins, despite evidence that hominin populations were pervasively structured and admixed.
AI.method: A conceptual critique identifying two blind spots in the current inferential pipeline: (1) the limitations imposed by data summarization, and (2) the practice gap where competing model classes are rarely fit to common data, with the proposal that this can be addressed by testing competing models against withheld summaries and transparently reporting rejected models.
AI.result: The paper identifies that the second blind spot is a matter of practice rather than data limitation, and offers concrete recommendations—testing against withheld summaries and reporting tried-and-rejected models—to narrow it.
AI.conclusion: Complexity, not simplicity, should be the appropriate prior for hominin population history, and researchers should adopt practices that better test and report competing model classes to resolve the complexity uncovered by ancient DNA evidence.

title: A weighted model of perception and decision-making between targets of finite size
summary: Recent research grounded in experiments has connected neural ring models of vision to how animals navigate a complex landscape of attractive targets. In this paper we investigate the mathematical and biological implications of a three-stage model where animals pre-process visual stimuli to identify a discrete set of targets, process this input to select the dominant targets, and then post-process this information to navigate the landscape. Incorporating finite target sizes and a neural density allows consistent target acquisition and pursuit reflecting what is seen in nature. Mathematically, we show this model corresponds to an energy minimization problem, simplifying both its analysis and numerical implementation. Biologically, we argue that the model is physiologically motivated, reproduces experimental observations, and presents a fairly direct pathway to decoding neural geometry via empirical data. Our results also demonstrate an analysis pipeline for future model extensions and suggest specific avenues for experimental research to test and parameterize our quantitative framework.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a three-stage neural model of visual navigation where animals pre-process visual stimuli to identify targets, select dominant targets through neural ring dynamics, and post-process this information to navigate. The model incorporates finite target sizes and neural density, corresponds to an energy minimization problem, and is shown to be physiologically motivated with a pathway to decoding neural geometry from empirical data.
AI.motivation: To extend neural ring models of vision from experimental contexts to a full three-stage mathematical framework that captures how animals navigate landscapes with multiple attractive targets, while making the model biologically plausible and mathematically tractable.
AI.method: The authors propose a three-stage model: (1) pre-processing visual stimuli to identify a discrete set of targets, (2) processing this input through neural ring dynamics to select dominant targets, and (3) post-processing to navigate the landscape. They incorporate finite target sizes and a neural density function, showing the model reduces to an energy minimization problem.
AI.result: The model yields consistent target acquisition and pursuit behaviors that reflect natural observations, simplifies analysis and numerical implementation through energy minimization, reproduces experimental observations, and provides an analysis pipeline for future model extensions.
AI.conclusion: The three-stage neural model is physiologically motivated, reproduces experimental data, offers a direct pathway for decoding neural geometry from empirical measurements, and suggests specific experimental avenues to test and parameterize the quantitative framework.

title: Dark energy: the cost of function in protein evolution
summary: The evolutionary fate of proteins is driven by both folding stability and biological function, dual constraints that often conflict, creating frustration and imposing functional costs beyond stability. These costs can be captured by a "dark energy": the difference between the evolutionary energy of protein sequences and their physical folding energy. Recent advances in deep mutational scanning, protein language models, and inverse-folding models have enabled the quantification of dark energy across the protein universe. We review the computational and experimental approaches that disentangle folding and function at scale, revealing a dark energy component and providing new insights into how biological information flows from sequence to structure to function and back to sequence.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews the concept of "dark energy" in proteins—the gap between evolutionary energy and physical folding energy—which quantifies the functional costs (frustration) incurred beyond stability. It surveys computational and experimental approaches using deep mutational scanning, protein language models, and inverse-folding models to disentangle folding and function constraints at scale, offering new insights into the bidirectional flow of biological information from sequence to structure to function and back.
AI.motivation: Proteins are constrained by two often-conflicting forces: folding stability and biological function. Understanding the evolutionary costs imposed by this duality is critical, but the functional burden beyond stability has been difficult to quantify. The paper aims to establish and review the "dark energy" framework as a way to measure this evolutionary-functional cost across the protein universe.
AI.method: The paper is a review that synthesizes recent advances in deep mutational scanning, protein language models, and inverse-folding models to quantify the difference between evolutionary energy and physical folding energy (dark energy). It consolidates computational and experimental approaches that enable large-scale disentanglement of folding constraints from functional constraints.
AI.result: The review reveals a measurable dark energy component in proteins, demonstrating that functional constraints impose evolutionary costs beyond what physical stability alone would predict. It shows that modern high-throughput and deep learning-based tools can quantify this component across the protein universe.
AI.conclusion: The dark energy framework provides a unifying lens for understanding how proteins balance stability and function under evolutionary pressure, and highlights how biological information flows bidirectionally—from sequence to structure to function and back to sequence—offering new avenues for protein engineering and evolutionary analysis.

title: Efficient Auto-Interpretability of AI Models in Biology
summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and other interpretability methods could turn AI models in Biology and other fields into engines of scientific discovery by explaining the superhuman capabilities of those models. However, a latent is only useful if we know three things: whether it is coherent, whether it can be described, and whether that description has predictive power. These questions are routinely conflated. We assemble them into a single pipeline and report the practical innovations each stage required. First, cross-seed dictionary stability prioritises which latents are worth spending resources to investigate. Second, an intruder-detection task asks whether a latents activating examples share a recognizable pattern. Third, a separate pass proposes a candidate biological description which we convert into falsifiable predictions which can be tested in silico. Deployed on the Boltz-1 Pairformer trunk, stability prioritisation finds interpretable latents using about 4.4 times fewer latent evaluations each, and at 5.2 times lower measured cost, while recovering over half of them, and the external check shows the surfaced motifs are significantly enriched for their claimed annotations. The results also suggest a possible tension: the cross- seed stability might be selecting for some types of features, like structure-related ones, much more than others, such as function-related features.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a three-stage pipeline for evaluating sparse autoencoder latents in biology-focused AI models: (1) cross-seed dictionary stability to prioritize promising latents, (2) an intruder-detection task to test latent coherence, and (3) candidate biological descriptions converted into falsifiable in silico predictions. Applied to the Boltz-1 Pairformer, the method reduces latent evaluations ~4.4x and cost ~5.2x while recovering over half of interpretable latents, though it may bias toward structure-related features over function-related ones.
AI.motivation: Interpretability methods like SAEs could enable scientific discovery from superhuman AI models in biology, but latents are only useful if we know whether they are coherent, describable, and predictively powerful. These three questions are routinely conflated, and no unified pipeline exists to address them systematically.
AI.method: The authors assemble three distinct evaluation stages into a single pipeline: (1) cross-seed dictionary stability to prioritize which latents deserve investigation, (2) an intruder-detection task to test whether a latent's activating examples share a recognizable pattern, and (3) a separate pass proposing candidate biological descriptions converted into falsifiable predictions testable in silico. This is deployed on the Boltz-1 Pairformer trunk.
AI.result: Stability prioritization finds interpretable latents using ~4.4x fewer latent evaluations and at 5.2x lower measured cost while recovering over half of them. External checks show surfaced motifs are significantly enriched for their claimed annotations. However, cross-seed stability may preferentially select structure-related features over function-related features, suggesting a possible tension.
AI.conclusion: The three-stage pipeline effectively separates and addresses the distinct questions of latent coherence, describability, and predictive power, enabling more efficient interpretability analysis of biology-focused AI models. However, the observed bias toward structure-related features suggests that stability-based prioritization may need refinement to ensure balanced coverage of function-related features.

title: Hydrodynamic theories of chemotaxis-driven invasion in proliferating cell populations
summary: Biased migration up chemical gradients and proliferation are fundamental drivers of collective invasion in several biological processes ranging from embryonic morphogenesis to cancer. Nonetheless, our understanding of how their interplay yields distinct invasion patterns remains incomplete. In this work, we propose a multiscale framework to systematically derive macroscopic hydrodynamic theories of cell invasion from a mesoscopic description of cells as biased self-propelled, interacting particles that proliferate. Our framework reveals how clump and stream invasion patterns emerge from the same kinetic equation under different asymptotic regimes of cell proliferation. Stream invasion is characteristic of cell populations in which proliferation balances cell motion. In contrast, clump invasion requires a separation of the hydrodynamic timescale of motion and the slower timescale of proliferation. By means of a multiple-scale approach, our analysis reveals that clump invasion is described as a slow evolution through a family of mass-dependent travelling-wave solutions. Overall, our work offers a novel approach to investigate multiscale regulation of cell invasion in systems where cell proliferation and collective invasion evolve on distinct timescales.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a multiscale framework that derives macroscopic hydrodynamic theories of cell invasion from a mesoscopic description of biased, self-propelled, proliferating particles. It shows that clump and stream invasion patterns emerge from the same kinetic equation under different proliferation timescales, with clump invasion described as slow evolution through mass-dependent travelling-wave solutions.
AI.motivation: While biased migration and proliferation are known to be fundamental drivers of collective invasion in processes like morphogenesis and cancer, the interplay between these two mechanisms and how they produce distinct invasion patterns remains incompletely understood.
AI.method: The authors develop a multiscale (bottom-up) framework that systematically derives macroscopic hydrodynamic theories from a mesoscopic kinetic description of cells as biased self-propelled, interacting, proliferating particles. They employ asymptotic analysis and a multiple-scale approach to examine different proliferation regimes relative to cell motion.
AI.result: The framework shows that stream invasion arises when proliferation balances cell motion, whereas clump invasion requires a separation of timescales where the hydrodynamic motion is faster than proliferation. Clump invasion is characterized mathematically as a slow evolution through a family of mass-dependent travelling-wave solutions.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a novel multiscale approach for investigating how the timescale separation between proliferation and collective motion regulates distinct invasion patterns, offering insight into systems where proliferation and invasion evolve on different timescales.

title: Expanding the Human Ancestry Ontology to include under-represented populations and ethnicities for broader utility in annotations
comment: 21 pages, 1 figure. To be submitted to Cell Press Patterns
summary: Successful discovery, integration and reuse of data relies on the availability of rich, well-structured and machine-readable metadata to describe every aspect of the data, from sample sources to collection processes to experimental protocols. The use of standardised terminologies to express concepts in a harmonised fashion lies at the core of high-quality data annotation, increasing the FAIRness of the data, facilitating data integration and promoting reproducibility. Here, we describe the Human Ancestry Ontology (HANCESTRO), originally developed to improve standardised reporting of genetic ancestry genomic resources such as the NHGRI-EBI GWAS Catalog and the Human Cell Atlas through high-level population descriptors, and more recently expanded to include diverse and previously under-represented populations in genomics and genetics research. HANCESTRO provides a framework for population descriptors that includes both ancestry based on the analysis of genetic information and self-reported ethnicity, which is based on social and cultural factors that don't necessarily align with genetic populations. By enabling the accurate and interoperable representation of population-related data, it promotes inclusive, representative and reproducible science.

AI.tldr: The paper describes the Human Ancestry Ontology (HANCESTRO), a standardized ontology developed to improve the reporting of genetic ancestry and population descriptors in genomics resources. It was originally created for the NHGRI-EBI GWAS Catalog and Human Cell Atlas but has been expanded to include diverse and underrepresented populations, covering both genetic ancestry and self-reported ethnicity.
AI.motivation: High-quality data annotation requires standardized terminologies to describe concepts harmoniously. The lack of standardized population descriptors in genomics research hinders data integration, FAIRness, and reproducibility. Existing resources needed a formal framework to represent genetic ancestry and ethnicity in an interoperable way, while also addressing the underrepresentation of diverse populations.
AI.method: The paper describes the development of HANCESTRO, an ontology providing high-level population descriptors and a framework that distinguishes between genetic ancestry (based on analysis of genetic information) and self-reported ethnicity (based on social and cultural factors). The ontology was initially built for the GWAS Catalog and Human Cell Atlas and later expanded to include diverse and underrepresented populations.
AI.result: HANCESTRO enables the accurate and interoperable representation of population-related data across genomic resources, promoting inclusive, representative, and reproducible science while facilitating data integration and FAIRness.
AI.conclusion: Standardized population descriptors via ontologies like HANCESTRO are essential for improving data quality, integration, and reproducibility in genomics, while also advancing inclusivity by representing diverse and underrepresented populations.

title: Linking individual bioenergetics to ecosystem dynamics with integral projection models
summary: Linking individual-level processes, such as survival and reproduction, to ecosystem dynamics is challenging due to interactions among populations and species. These interactions depend on organism traits, such as age, body size, and mass, and are influenced by fluctuations in population structure. Integral projection models (IPMs) have advanced our understanding of dynamics arising from population structure in continuous traits. Yet, these models have only been applied to relatively simple systems, featuring one or two species and spanning a fraction of the trophic levels observed in natural food webs. We extend these models in four ways. First, we provide a general multi-species IPM where population structure can be included in primary producers and primary and secondary consumers. Second, we link individual-level processes to ecosystem functioning by mapping fluxes of biomass between species to fluxes within individuals, using bioenergetic principles for allocation to maintenance, reproduction, or growth. Third, we introduce a nutrient recycling loop through which decomposers break down organic matter into nutrients that enable plant growth. Finally, we provide an efficient fitting algorithm to calibrate the model with time series of population sizes. We showcase our approach by parameterising and fitting the model to counts of elk, bison, wolves, and cougars in northern Yellowstone National Park to study the impact of predator extirpation and recovery. Our model predicts that bison decrease following predator removal and recover following predator recovery, suggesting a positive contribution of wolves and cougars to the increase of bison in northern Yellowstone. It also reproduces indirect effects of predators on woody deciduous vegetation regeneration. Our approach is suitable for a broad range of ecosystems, with applications for population management and ecological forecasting.

AI.tldr: This paper extends integral projection models (IPMs) to multi-species, multi-trophic-level ecosystems, linking individual-level processes to ecosystem dynamics and functioning. The approach incorporates bioenergetic principles, nutrient recycling via decomposers, and an efficient fitting algorithm. The model is demonstrated on Yellowstone National Park data (elk, bison, wolves, cougars), predicting predator-mediated effects on bison populations and indirect effects on vegetation.
AI.motivation: Traditional IPMs are limited to one or two species and a fraction of trophic levels found in natural food webs, preventing a link between individual-level processes (survival, reproduction, growth) and ecosystem-level dynamics.
AI.method: The authors extend IPMs in four ways: (1) a general multi-species IPM with population structure across primary producers and primary/secondary consumers; (2) linking individual-level processes to ecosystem functioning by mapping biomass fluxes between species to fluxes within individuals via bioenergetic allocation (maintenance, reproduction, growth); (3) introducing a nutrient recycling loop where decomposers break down organic matter into nutrients for plant growth; (4) providing an efficient fitting algorithm to calibrate the model with time series of population sizes.
AI.result: When parameterised and fitted to Yellowstone data (elk, bison, wolves, cougars), the model predicts that bison decrease following predator removal and recover following predator recovery, suggesting a positive contribution of predators to bison increase. The model also reproduces indirect effects of predators on woody deciduous vegetation regeneration.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework is applicable across a broad range of ecosystems and has practical value for population management and ecological forecasting.

title: Adaptive self-organized criticality in deep neural networks
summary: Deep neural networks are high-dimensional dynamical systems whose function depends on the stable propagation of activity and perturbations across many layers. Maintaining suitable dynamical regimes may therefore be essential for robust learning and for preventing dynamical instabilities during training. Here, we show that the global dynamical state of a deep neural network can be autonomously regulated by purely local homeostatic plasticity. Neuronal activity is inferred from responses across inputs, and individual synapses are strengthened or weakened using only the activity of their postsynaptic neuron. Without measuring any global network property, this rule drives networks from both subcritical and supercritical initial conditions toward a common critical state, characterized by conserved activity propagation and a vanishing largest finite-time Lyapunov exponent. When combined with gradient-based learning, homeostatic adaptation counteracts the training-induced drift toward supercritical dynamics, while revealing a competition between dynamical regulation and task optimization. Our results demonstrate how adaptive self-organization can be implemented in deep neural networks and how local plasticity can control their collective dynamical operating point.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that local homeostatic plasticity—where individual synapses are adjusted based only on their postsynaptic neuron's activity—can autonomously regulate the global dynamical state of deep neural networks, driving them toward a critical state with conserved activity propagation and vanishing Lyapunov exponents, and counteracting training-induced drift toward supercritical dynamics.
AI.motivation: Deep neural networks are high-dimensional dynamical systems whose stability depends on propagating activity and perturbations reliably across layers. Maintaining appropriate dynamical regimes is essential for robust learning and preventing instabilities, but it is unclear whether such regulation can be achieved autonomously through purely local mechanisms without measuring global network properties.
AI.method: The authors propose a local homeostatic plasticity rule in which neuronal activity is inferred from responses across inputs, and individual synapses are strengthened or weakened using only the activity of their postsynaptic neuron. This purely local rule is tested on networks from both subcritical and supercritical initial conditions, and is also combined with gradient-based learning to examine the interaction between dynamical regulation and task optimization.
AI.result: The local homeostatic rule drives networks from both subcritical and supercritical initial states toward a common critical state, characterized by conserved activity propagation and a vanishing largest finite-time Lyapunov exponent. When combined with gradient-based learning, homeostatic adaptation counteracts training-induced drift toward supercritical dynamics, revealing a competition between dynamical regulation and task optimization.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate how adaptive self-organization can be implemented in deep neural networks and show that purely local synaptic plasticity can control the collective dynamical operating point of the network, potentially providing a biologically plausible mechanism for maintaining stable yet expressive dynamics during learning.
